speaker: Mario Zechner
main_topic: Building a custom, minimal, and self-modifying coding agent called 'pi' to counter the bloat and unpredictability of current commercial coding agents, and a critique of the AI-generated 'slop' negatively impacting software development and open source.
key_claims: Commercial coding agents like Claude Code become bloated, buggy, and unpredictable as they add unnecessary features.
The industry is currently in the 'fuck around and find out' phase of coding agents.
Developers need self-modifying, malleable agents that adapt to their specific workflows, rather than forcing developers to adapt to the agent.
Current agents use excessive token budgets for system prompts and tools, whereas a minimal approach is sufficient because frontier models are already trained to act as coding agents.
AI coding agents generate massive amounts of code quickly, creating a bottleneck for human review and leading to compounding errors ('booboos').
Automated agents ('clankers') are degrading the open-source ecosystem by spamming repositories with low-quality issues and pull requests.
Agents learn architectural complexity and bad practices from the vast amount of mediocre code on the internet.
A 'sufficiently detailed spec' is just a program; leaving blanks in specs causes agents to fill them with mediocre internet-learned code.
Agents should not be used for mission-critical code or architectural decisions; humans must retain agency and write critical code by hand.
Developers need to slow down, say no to unnecessary features, and use agents for scoped, non-critical tasks rather than full automation.

frameworks.name: Pi Architecture Packages
components: pi-ai: Unified LLM API, 15+ providers, streaming, tool calling, cross-provider context handoff.
pi-agent-core: Agent loop, tool execution, validation, event streaming, message queuing.
pi-tui: Terminal UI framework, differential rendering, synchronized output, (almost) flicker-free.
pi-coding-agent: The CLI. Session management, themes, extensions, skills, project context.

frameworks.name: Properties of good agent tasks
components: Scoped such that agent doesn't need to gobble up tons of code
Closed loop: agent can evaluate its own work
Boring stuff, or things you'd never have time to try
Rubber duck to bounce ideas against in lieu of human
You evaluate, take what's reasonable, finalize

examples.lesson: Behind-the-scenes modifications to the system prompt and inopportune system reminders break developer workflows and cause model confusion.

examples.example: OpenCode context handling and LSP integration
examples.lesson: Aggressive pruning of tool outputs 'lobotomizes' the model, and injecting LSP errors immediately after edits confuses models that don't expect instant feedback mid-thought.
A hyper-minimal harness sending keystrokes to tmux outperforms native bloated harnesses, proving that frontier models naturally know how to act as coding agents without massive toolsets.
By providing a minimal core, documentation, and a hot-reloading extension system, an agent can build its own tools and adapt to the user's workflow.

AI agents are generating so much automated noise that open-source maintainers must build specific filters (like demanding a 'human voice' or using 'vouch' systems) to manage the influx of garbage PRs.
Claiming a product is entirely built by AI is a red flag for poor quality, as agents lack the taste, understanding, and pain-avoidance mechanisms of human developers, leading to broken software.

terminology.definition: Unwanted, low-quality, or excessive AI-generated content, specifically code that degrades the overall quality of a project.
Automated AI agents or bots that autonomously interact with systems, often spamming open-source repositories with low-quality issues and pull requests.
The speaker's term for errors or bugs introduced by AI coding agents, which compound rapidly due to the speed of generation.
Coding agents that can be easily modified, extended, and even modify themselves to fit a developer's specific workflow.
Terminal User Interface; the text-based interface used by CLI coding agents.
Language Server Protocol; used to provide auto-complete and error-checking, which can confuse agents if injected improperly during generation.

takeaways: Stop adapting to bloated commercial coding agents; take control and build or use minimal tools that fit your specific workflow.
Frontier LLMs are already trained to be coding agents; you don't need massive system prompts and complex toolsets to get them to code.
The speed at which agents generate code far outpaces human review capacity, leading to compounding errors and unmaintainable codebases.
Do not trust agents with mission-critical code or architectural decisions; human friction and pain are necessary for learning and maintaining system integrity.
Protect open-source projects from 'clankers' by implementing human-verification steps and ruthlessly filtering AI-generated spam.
Slow down, exercise discipline, say no to unnecessary features, and use agents for scoped, non-critical tasks to polish the right features.

notable_quotes.quote: I build pi in a world of slop and this is a tragedy in three acts.
The real problem is that my context wasn't my context.
We are in the fuck around and find out phase of coding agents.
We need better ways to fuck around: self-modifying, malleable agents.
Adapt your coding agent to your workflows, not the other way around.
You don't need 10,000 tokens to tell them you are a coding agent. They know, because they are coding agents now.
Clankers are destroying OSS as we know it.
Agents are actually compounding booboos, which is my word for errors, with zero learning and no bottlenecks.
Agents are merchants of learned complexity.
Know what we call a sufficiently detailed spec? It's a program.
Slow the fuck down. Think about what you're building and why.

statistics: Pi uses < 1,000 tokens for its system prompt and tool definitions.
Codex uses ~3,000 tokens for its system prompt.
OpenCode uses ~7,000 tokens for its system prompt.
Claude Code uses ~10,000 tokens for its system prompt.
The OpenClaw repository received over 5,000 issues and 5,000 pull requests, heavily attributed to bot spam.
Enterprise-grade complexity can be reached in 2 weeks with 2 humans and 10 agents.
A news headline mentioned Microsoft CEO claiming up to 30% of the company's code was written by AI.
